title: Library Management
brief: Design the class structure for a library management system. The system tracks books, members, and loans. You are designing the object model — not the UI or persistence.

requirements.text: Books have immutable bibliographic data and a mutable availability status.
Members can borrow up to a limited number of books concurrently.
Loans record the book, member, loan date, and due date; they cannot be altered after creation.
When a book is returned, its availability status is updated and any overdue fine is calculated.
The system must prevent borrowing a book that is already loaned out.

constraints: Single-threaded operations; one transaction at a time
No persistence layer; data lives in memory
Only books and members; no multimedia items

variationPoints.name: borrowing policy
variationPoints.why: Loan limits and loan periods differ by member type — students, staff, visitors — and change with the academic calendar

variationPoints.name: fine calculation policy
variationPoints.why: Libraries may use a flat fee or a per‑day rate for overdue items

scenarios.title: Member borrows an available book
scenarios.description: Member selects a book, the system creates a loan and marks the book as unavailable. Walk through which objects act.

scenarios.title: Member returns a book on time
scenarios.description: Member returns a previously borrowed book, the system updates availability and records no fine. Walk through the steps.

scenarios.title: Member attempts to borrow a loaned-out book
scenarios.description: Member selects a book that is already loaned, the system refuses the operation. Walk through the failure path.

hiddenChanges.prompt: The library is introducing member types. Students may hold 3 books for 14 days; staff may hold 10 for 30; visitors may hold 1 for 7 and may not renew. Revise your design so each type's limits apply when a member borrows — and say what you touched and why.
goodSignal: adds one policy class per member type behind an abstraction the library already held
the borrow walkthrough is unchanged apart from which policy answers
names where the loan period comes from now
badSignal: adds a memberType flag and branches on it
puts the limits inside Member or Library as conditionals
changes Loan or Book to absorb it

hiddenChanges.prompt: The library wants a tiered fine policy: a grace period, then a per‑day rate up to a maximum cap. Update the design to accommodate this — and explain what you changed.
goodSignal: creates a new fine policy implementation class
parameterizes fine calculation without altering existing policies
expresses grace period and caps in the new class
badSignal: uses if‑else inside existing fine calculation method

probes.prompt: When a member attempts to borrow a book, which class decides whether the loan can be created — {{class}}, or something else — and how many places would you have to check to be sure?
goodSignal: names one class that owns the answer

probes.prompt: {{class}} holds loan records, member data and fine calculations. Which of those three would you extract first, and who would call it afterwards?
goodSignal: names one responsibility and its new owner

probes.prompt: A member tries to loan a book that is already on loan. Which class knows that, when does it discover the conflict, and what does the user see?
goodSignal: names a refusal the customer sees

probes.prompt: Is the fine stored as an integer in your design? If so, what cannot be expressed — and does it affect exact fine calculation?
goodSignal: names denominations or currency as the thing lost

probes.prompt: A member asks for a due-date extension. Loans cannot be altered after creation — so which class produces the new state, what happens to the old Loan, and who else has to know?
goodSignal: names one class that creates a replacement or a new loan
says what the old record becomes
names the caller that must see the new due date
badSignal: mutates the due date in place
cannot say where the extension is decided

commonFailureModes.name: Mutable bibliographic data
commonFailureModes.description: Book class allows title or ISBN to be changed after creation, breaking immutability.

commonFailureModes.name: God object Library
commonFailureModes.description: A single Library class holds books, members, and loans and performs all logic, violating cohesion.

commonFailureModes.name: Direct collection exposure
commonFailureModes.description: Internal lists of books or members are returned directly, allowing external modification.

strong.tradeoffs: BookLookup and BookPersistence split catalog responsibilities, enabling independent read/write implementations; FinePolicy implementations are now concrete strategies; Library depends only on interfaces, improving testability and swapping implementations.

decisions.what: Keep borrowing logic in Library rather than a separate service
decisions.why: Keeps model simple for the given scope

critiquePairs.question: Next term, students and staff get different loan limits. Which design absorbs that without editing working code? Click the class that makes it possible.
critiquePairs.telling: On the left, the limit is an answer the Library asks for — BorrowingPolicy.canBorrow — so a second member type is a second class that answers differently, and borrowBook does not change. On the right, the limit is a number inside Library.borrowBook, and a second type is a branch inside the method that already works. The design that can say who decides in one place is the one that survives the change.

critiquePairs.question: Which design keeps the Library class focused, avoiding it knowing fine‑calculation details?
critiquePairs.telling: In the mutable‑bibliographic‑data design the Library collaborates with a FinePolicy interface, delegating all fine calculations. Library’s responsibility stays limited to orchestrating loans and members. In the god‑object‑library design the Library also contains the fine‑calculation logic, bloating its responsibilities and violating the Single‑Responsibility Principle.
